ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows the z-axis vertical upward and the x-axis horizontal to the right. The circular turn is drawn as an ellipse because of perspective, with its diameter aligned along the x-axis. The two terminals on the right are labeled V_turn. The magnetic field intensity arrow H points upward, parallel to the +z direction. Reasoning: Since the loop revolves about its x-axis diameter, its area vector rotates relative to the uniform magnetic field along +z, so the magnetic flux through the single turn varies sinusoidally. Given r = 1 m, area A = pi r^2 = pi m^2. The field intensity is H = 10^7 A/m and mu0 = 4pi x 10^-7, so B = mu0 H = 4pi T. The rotation speed is 60 rpm = 1 revolution/s, hence omega = 2pi rad/s. For sinusoidal flux Phi = B A cos(omega t), the peak induced voltage is |dPhi/dt|_max = B A omega. Therefore V_peak = (4pi)(pi)(2pi) = 8 pi^3 = 248.05 V.

method.method_draft: Describe the image geometry first: the field arrow is along +z and the loop rotates about its x-axis diameter, so the magnetic flux through the single turn varies sinusoidally as its area vector rotates. From the text take r=1 m, speed=60 rpm, mu0=4 pi x 10^-7, and H=10^7 A/m. Convert H to B: B=mu0 H=4 pi T. Convert 60 rpm to omega=2 pi rad/s. Compute the turn area A=pi(1)^2. Apply Faraday's law and take the maximum derivative of the sinusoidal flux: V_peak=B A omega=(4 pi)(pi)(2 pi)=8 pi^3=248.05 V.

method.method_draft: Parameterize the circular turn as a radius-R circle whose one diameter is along x and whose transverse radius direction rotates about x. For a point on the loop, use v=omega x_hat × r. Insert the uniform field B=mu0 H z_hat into the motional-emf integral V=∮(v×B)·dl. The angular dependence integrates to ∫0^{2pi} sin^2 phi dphi=pi, giving an instantaneous emf proportional to B omega R^2 pi times a sinusoidal orientation factor; hence the peak is V_peak=B omega pi R^2. Substitute R=1 m, omega=2 pi rad/s from 60 rpm, and B=(4 pi x 10^-7)(10^7)=4 pi T to get V_peak=(4 pi)(2 pi)(pi)=248.05 V.
